title: Re: OpenAI discloses four more rogue incidents...
text:
"OpenAI says it has since improved its security as well as its alignment grading. “In response to this and to other incidents, we’ve strengthened our security controls, blocked models from accessing the live internet during training or evaluation, improved our alignment grading, and extended our misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic,” the company noted."

----------------

They're not doing an acceptable job of regulating themselves. Their peers can't/won't do anything. The U.S. government certainly isn't going to do anything that might pop the bubble. Technical solutions like blocking traffic from OpenAI will likely not work.

What recourse does the public have? Victims can sue, but companies like OpenAI could pay out a few hundred million and call it a rounding error. Settlements may happen, but the incidents will continue.

title: Show HN: Gridmark – make logos by tweaking shapes on a grid
text:
I built this (with claude) as i needed a logo for a project im working on but really did not want to use AI to make the logo. It all runs in browser and you can make logos and save them and download png and svgs without watermarks or anything.

At the end of the day it's just an SVG manipulator with some sensible bounds for making some pretty cool looking designs.

I did add a paid feature to download the whole brand kit but not really looking to make any money out of it. Would love feedback or any ideas on things to add for different grid types / styles.

title: Show HN: Sys2txt – transcribe system audio to text in the CLI with a local LLM
text:
sys2txt is a command line tool that records whatever audio your Linux machine is playing (via PulseAudio/PipeWire's monitor source) and transcribes it live with Whisper, OpenAI's AI-based speech-to-text model.

I use it to caption meetings, videos, and calls playing on my own machine without routing audio through anything else. It supports faster-whisper, openai-whisper, and whisper.cpp (with Vulkan GPU support for AMD), and can either record-then-transcribe once or stream continuously in segments with live output in txt/srt/vtt/json/tsv.

I'd be keen to collaborate with others extend its functionality to other operating systems and hardware.

(I have been using and developing this tool since November 2025.)

title: Re: Ask HN: What is the most useful thing AI has done ...
text:
It's hard to discriminate out just one specific thing, but a batch of generally connected stuff:

1. I've been doing a lot of experimenting with neuromorphic and analog computing. ChatGPT has been my research assistant / lab partner throughout and has helped with doing experiment write-ups, analyzing scope waveforms (it's really impressive how good it is at parsing screnshots from the scope, using the graticule / divisions, and other on-screen indicators to figure things out), finding reference material, and providing general electronics advice. I've learned a TON of new stuff about using my oscilloscope, using some features I'd never used before.[1]

2. Along with that, I'd long wanted to get my lab all set up to use LXI for remotely controlling all (well, "most") of my test equipment. Once I did the work of physically connecting all of the instruments to the LAN, ChatGPT wrote most of the first cut of a batch of Python programs using PyVISA to control the various instruments (oscilloscope, function generator, power supply, multimeter, programmable load) and to download data from them.

3. I'd been "meaning to learn KiCAD one day" for about 15 years. About a month ago I said something to that effect to ChatGPT and it handily replied "I can help you with that." About 6 or 7 hours later I was sending Gerbers to JLCPCB with my first custom PCB design, and 4 days later I had my first boards in my hand. Soldered one up and it worked first time! Yay. Now granted, the circuit was VERY simple (a 555 timer blinking an LED) but the point was to learn the tool and the workflow, not the actual end product. About two weeks later I started on my second board, planning to do it with much less AI assistance (I worry a lot about cognitive abdication / brain-rot / etc). But right out of the gate, I ran into the point that KiCAD did not have a symbol for an obsolete component I was using (the 2N6027 PUT). So I turned to ChatGPT again and it helped me create a custom symbol. After that little diversion, I went back to the schematic and board layout. This time around, it only took about 85 "turns" with the AI to get to "Gerbers sent to JLCPCB" whereas the first time it took about 120 "turns". So I'm feeling pretty good that I am actually learning and retaining some of this knowledge and not "just following instructions from the AI". I do hope to get to the point soon of doing a board with NO assistance from the AI whatsoever.

Those are the ones that stand to me. There's other stuff of course, but those are ones that have really made a difference for me and/or really impressed me.

[1]: One thing I did that helped a lot, was creating a "Project" and uploading all of the user manuals and programming guides for my various instruments. So the GPT always has access to the actual documentation and doesn't have to rely on its "memory".
